svg.text: How a car answers the wheel

Two cars, identical in every way except how far their weight sits from the middle. Both are given the same 1° flick of steering at 20 m/s, at the same instant. Each frame is the heading each car has turned to by that moment.
Weight near the middle · 0.75× polar moment
Both cars weigh the same and carry the same share of it over the front wheels. The only difference is whether that weight sits near the
middle or out at the ends — and it is worth 130 ms of delay before the car starts doing what you asked.
The one with its weight spread out is slower to start turning, and slightly steadier once it gets there — it overshoots a little less.
Both effects are small on this car, because a bicycle model is almost critically damped: it has none of the tire and suspension lag that
makes a real car swing past by 5-40%. Trust the direction here, not the size.
Both end up in exactly the same corner. Polar moment changes the journey, never the destination.

[MEASURED] bicycle model + Sedan_Pac02Tire.tir · offsets removed · m 1360 kg · Izz 1950 kg·m² · 54% front · [SOURCED] RV-1 parameters, vehicle-reference-parameters.md §1 · step steer 1° at 20 m/s [ASSUMED] · inertia multipliers 0.75-1.40 [SOURCED range, §2]

Heading is the integral of yaw rate, drawn to scale. This is the axis Episode 8 is about, and it is independent of weight distribution: two cars can be balanced identically and still answer completely differently.
